Chapter One: Growing Up in Hard Times and Finding Early Purpose
Imagine stepping out into the fields of rural Arkansas, where the world feels both endless and a little bit closed in. For a kid whose family works the land as sharecroppers, life’s all about early mornings and long, hard days. The sun’s barely up when the work begins, and it’s late before anyone finally gets to rest. Out here, survival isn’t just about one person’s effort—it’s a team sport, and every single family member, even the youngest, has to pitch in.
Home is about as simple as it gets. It’s built for necessity, not for comfort. There’s this strong feeling of togetherness, but at the same time, you can almost sense the constant worry in the air—worry about the next harvest, about paying bills, about what the next day might bring.
The father is a tough man, driven by a belief in hard work above all else. He expects everyone to follow his example, to work hard, and not to complain. The mother, on the other hand, is gentle but incredibly strong. She’s the glue that holds everything together, holding onto her faith and steady presence. Even when things get tough, she’ll hum a hymn while working, her voice bringing comfort and a spark of hope to the whole family.
Music isn’t just something in the background—it’s woven into every part of daily life. You hear it in church on Sundays, in the melodies sung while working, and in those rare quiet moments when the family gathers around an old radio. For one child, music becomes much more than a soundtrack—it’s a lifeline, a way to understand the world and to dream about something bigger than the cotton fields.
School offers a short escape from the farm’s demands, but it isn’t always easy. There’s always that feeling of being different, always carrying the weight of struggle and hardship. Still, there’s a fierce determination to learn, to dive into books and stories, and to imagine a life that’s different from what’s expected.
Then, tragedy hits early. The sudden loss of a beloved sibling shakes the family to its core. Grief settles over the home, and nothing feels the same. The father, already strict, becomes even more distant, his pain turning inward. The mother leans even harder on her faith, finding comfort in prayer and song. For the child left behind, that loss becomes a driving force—a reminder of just how fragile life is, and how important it is to make every moment count.
As the teenage years approach, the pull of music only grows stronger. There’s a sense that music might just offer a way out, a path toward something bigger. The first guitar arrives as a gift, and with it comes endless hours of practice. Sure, the fingers ache, but the spirit soars. Songs are picked up by ear, borrowed from the radio or remembered from church. Every new chord feels like a small victory, a step closer to a dream that still feels impossibly far away.
The world outside that small town calls out, but it’s intimidating. There’s a longing to see what’s beyond the horizon, but also a fear of leaving behind everything that’s familiar. The family’s struggles, the lessons learned out in the fields, and the memories of loss—they all become part of the foundation for whatever comes next.
Through all the ups and downs, faith is a constant companion. It’s not always easy to believe, especially when things are hard, but there’s a quiet sense that something bigger is at work. The hymns sung in church, the prayers at night, and those quiet moments of reflection—they all help keep hope alive.
Looking back, it’s clear these early years—marked by struggle, loss, and the search for meaning—are what truly shape the person to come. The lessons learned in the fields, the strength found in family, and the comfort discovered through music and faith—they all become the building blocks for a life that’s destined to be anything but ordinary.
